content: GemIdent is an interactive image processing program designed to identify regions of interest within images. It is particularly effective for images with a limited number of colors, where the objects of interest exhibit similar appearances with minor variations. For instance, it can be used for color image segmentation tasks such as distinguishing oranges on a tree or identifying stained cells in microscopic images. Additionally, GemIdent includes data analysis tools to explore spatial relationships among the identified objects. GemIdent was developed at Stanford University by Adam Kapelner between June 2006 and January 2007 in the laboratory of Dr. Peter Lee, under the guidance of Professor Susan Holmes. The concept for the program was inspired by data from a publication on immune profiles of lymph nodes in breast cancer patients. Consequently, GemIdent is particularly well-suited for identifying cells in immunohistochemically (IHC)-stained tissue imaged via automated light microscopy, especially when the nuclear background stain and membrane/cytoplasmic stain are clearly defined. The methodology of GemIdent relies on supervised learning to automate the identification of regions of interest in images. Users are required to perform initial tasks, such as providing relevant colors and marking examples of the objects or regions of interest, as well as negatives, to create a training set. When a user clicks on a pixel, the program generates multiple scores based on surrounding color information using Mahalanobis Ring Score attribute generation. These scores are then used to construct a random forest machine-learning classifier, which classifies pixels in any given image. If classification errors occur, users can return to the training phase, identify specific mistakes, and reclassify the image. This iterative process of training, classifying, retraining, and reclassifying—referred to as interactive boosting—can result in highly accurate segmentation. The source code for GemIdent is available for non-commercial users and is written in pure Java 6. However, the code is licensed under the GemIdent license, which was created by Stanford's Office of Technology and Licensing. This license is not an open-source or free software license, as it prohibits commercial redistribution and imposes significant restrictions on the distribution of derivative works. Examples of GemIdent's capabilities include the following: A raw photograph of oranges on a tree can be processed to produce a superimposed mask showing pixel classification results, and the final image can be marked with the centroids of the identified oranges. A raw microscopic image of a stained lymph node from the Kohrt study can be processed to generate a superimposed mask showing pixel classification results, and the final image can be marked with the centroids of cancer nuclei. GemIdent can also identify multiple phenotypes within the same image. For example, in a stained lymph node image, it can classify cancer nuclei (marked with green stars), T-cells (yellow stars), and non-specific background nuclei (cyan stars). The program also includes a command-line data analysis and visualization interface. This interface can analyze classification results, such as the distribution of distances from T-cells to neighboring cancer cells, as displayed in a histogram. Additionally, binary images of cancer membranes can be generated as a result of pixel-only classification. An autogenerated PDF report of the analysis is also available, which includes a thumbnail view of the entire lymph node, counts and Type I error rates for all phenotypes, and a transcript of the analyses performed.
